geography.title: French Flanders: minority language and editorial display revision
geography.citation: French Ministry of Culture; CNRS MoDyCo Entrelangues; ANVT–ILRF
geography.usedFor: Removed the atlas Dutch/Flemish solid footprint only inside the Natural Earth France boundary. The existing French reference background is visible there. A French Flemish peerd point at Quaëdypre preserves minority-language presence without inventing a modern majority-speaking boundary. Dutch/Flemish areas outside France are unchanged. This is an editorial display choice, not a new census or an assertion that Flemish has disappeared.

provenanceNotes: Colours follow displayed etymological routes. The PIE horse noun has separate Scottish Gaelic, Iranian and Greek routes. Caballus has separate Romance, Celtic and Albanian routes. In Greece, Russia and Kazakhstan, diagonal stripes show coexisting words with different origins in the same language area; the stripe proportions are decorative, not usage statistics. Small colour bars beneath those word labels identify their respective roots.

Wiktionary is a community-edited secondary reference. Entries are linked individually, with institutional and primary lexical sources for key unusual varieties. Research records and the source catalog retain the distinction between checked forms and unresolved deeper histories.

An asterisk marks a reconstructed form. The legend uses “loan ?” for a possible borrowing. Other uncertainties, including disputed deeper origins and early borrowing directions, are explained in the entry notes rather than abbreviated in the legend. The origin of caballus/*kaballos and the deeper origin of English horse are disputed. Finnic *hëpo is not automatically merged with PIE *h₁éḱwos. Early Iranian relationships proposed for Caucasian horse words remain proposals. No indigenous Canarian horse word was verified; that label and its historical island-reference fill are omitted, leaving the modern Spanish reference layer. The former snow gloss tener? is not reused.

Most language-area geography is reused from the snow atlas. The Hungarian footprint inside Romania is replaced by an explicitly selected 2021 mother-tongue census supplement, Algeria has a country-specific vernacular lexical join, French Flanders uses the French reference background with a Flemish minority point, and existing Mansi, Khanty and Caspian Iranian aggregates have documented lexical joins. North African Arabic and Berber word histories are reviewed separately. Community corrections and their sources were checked on 2026-10-19.
